nameStory: The name 'citronella horse balm' comes from the lovely lemon scent of its flowers, reminiscent of citronella plants. 'Horse balm' refers to its traditional use as a healing remedy for horses and other livestock. Some folks also call it 'richweed' because it grows in nutrient-rich soils, or 'stoneroot' for its preference for rocky ground.
description: Citronella horse balm is a tall, sturdy member of the mint family that can reach up to 4 feet high. It has large, toothed leaves and produces clusters of tiny yellow tubular flowers at the top of its stems in mid-summer. This woodland wildflower stands out because it blooms when most other forest flowers have finished for the season. Like other mint family members, it has a square stem, but it's much taller and more robust than most of its relatives.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow tubular flowers arranged in loose, branching clusters at the stem tips, with a delightful lemony fragrance that's especially noticeable on warm summer days

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, broad oval leaves with sharp teeth along the edges, arranged in pairs opposite each other on the stem, feeling somewhat rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright, growing 3-4 feet high with a sturdy, square mint-family stem that feels distinctly four-sided when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Bloom Timing
idTips.description: Flowers appear in mid to late summer when most woodland wildflowers have finished blooming, making it a standout in the shaded forest

habitat: Look for citronella horse balm in rich, moist woodlands, especially areas with rocky or limestone-rich soils. It thrives in the dappled shade of mature deciduous forests where the soil stays consistently moist and fertile. You'll often find it growing alongside other woodland plants like wild ginger and mayapple in these nutrient-rich forest floors.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the ground as large, wrinkled leaves begin to unfurl. The plant focuses on growing tall and establishing its substantial leafy structure.
seasonality.summer: The signature lemon-scented yellow flowers bloom from mid to late summer, typically July through August, creating a sweet citrusy fragrance in the forest air.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to die back, with leaves turning brown and withering as the first frosts arrive.
seasonality.winter: The entire above-ground portion dies back completely, leaving no visible trace until spring returns.

funFact: This plant is like the forest's natural air freshener! When most woodland flowers have finished blooming and summer heat makes forests feel stuffy, citronella horse balm fills the shady woods with its refreshing lemon scent, earning it the nickname 'nature's summer potpourri.'
confusionNotes: Its large toothed leaves might remind you of nettles at first glance, but citronella horse balm lacks the stinging hairs and has that distinctive lemony flower fragrance. The square stem and opposite leaves immediately mark it as a mint family member, not a nettle.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this isn't the same plant as commercial citronella used in bug repellent candles, though both share that lovely lemony scent. The 'horse balm' name reflects its folk medicine heritage, when people used it to treat wounds and ailments in their livestock.
compareHints: Citronella horse balm is the only member of its genus (Collinsonia) found in New England, making it unique among our local plants. Within the mint family, it's much taller and more robust than most relatives like wild bergamot or self-heal, and it's the only one with that distinctive lemon-scented yellow flower cluster. Its summer blooming time also sets it apart from most other woodland mints.
